name: Red Fort (Lal Qila)
description: An iconic 17th-century Mughal fortress constructed from red sandstone that served as the primary residence of Mughal emperors for nearly two centuries.
history: Commissioned in 1638 by Emperor Shah Jahan when he shifted the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi (Shahjahanabad). Designed by architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori and completed in 1648, the fort witnessed the zenith of Mughal glory, Nadir Shah's 1739 plunder of the Peacock Throne, British colonial transformation after the 1857 Rebellion, and the 1945 INA trials. On 15 August 1947, Jawaharlal Nehru unfurled the National Flag from Lahori Gate, starting an annual Independence Day tradition.

location: Netaji Subhash Marg, Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi
best_time: October to March (9:00 AM – 11:00 AM or 6:30 PM Sound & Light Show)

name: Qutab Minar
description: A 72.5-meter tall five-storey fluted minaret made of red sandstone and marble, representing early Indo-Islamic architectural supremacy.
history: Initiated in 1199 AD by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, founder of the Delhi Sultanate, following the defeat of the Tomar Rajputs. Sultan Shams-ud-din Iltutmish added three storeys around 1220. Following lightning damage in 1368, Sultan Firoz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the upper levels using white marble and sandstone. The complex also features the rust-resistant 4th-century Iron Pillar of Chandragupta II and the 1311 Alai Darwaza.

name: Humayun's Tomb
description: The first grand garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent, combining Persian symmetry with Indian stone carving traditions.
history: Commissioned in 1558 by Empress Bega Begum (Haji Begum) in memory of her late husband, Emperor Humayun. Designed by Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and completed in 1572, it introduced the Persian Charbagh (four-fold garden) concept with causeways and geometric water channels to India. It provided shelter to the last Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah Zafar before his capture by the British in 1857.

name: Purana Qila (Old Fort)
description: An imposing 16th-century fortress standing on an ancient mound historically associated with Indraprastha from the Mahabharata epic.
history: Rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri after defeating Humayun in 1540, completing the Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque and the octagonal Sher Mandal library tower. Humayun regained control in 1555 but fatally fell down the steep stone stairs of Sher Mandal in 1556. Archaeological excavations led by B.B. Lal revealed Painted Grey Ware pottery dating back to 1000 BCE, linking the site directly to ancient Indraprastha. During the 1947 Partition, it functioned as a major refugee camp.

name: Tughlaqabad Fort
description: A massive, ruined stone fortress spanning over 6 km with monumental sloping stone ramparts, battlements, and the mausoleum of Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq.
history: Built between 1321 and 1325 AD by Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, as the fortified third city of Delhi to repel Mongol incursions. Legend recounts that Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya cursed the fort ('Ya rahey hissar, ya basey Gujjar' — may it remain barren or inhabited only by nomadic Gujjars) after the Sultan requisitioned workers who were digging the saint's stepwell. The fortress was abandoned shortly after Ghiyas-ud-din's demise.

name: Feroz Shah Kotla Fort
description: The 14th-century citadel of Firozabad featuring the 3rd-century BCE Ashokan Stone Pillar, Jama Masjid ruins, and a circular stepped baoli.
history: Constructed in 1354 AD by Sultan Firoz Shah Tughlaq when he founded Firozabad, the fifth city of Delhi, alongside the Yamuna river. Firoz Shah transported a 13-meter monolithic polished sandstone Ashokan Pillar from Topra in Haryana and installed it atop a three-tier pyramidal palace. In 1398, Timur prayed at the Kotla Jama Masjid before sacking Delhi, later modeling his Samarkand mosque upon its design. Today, it is revered by locals who leave letters and petitions to Djinns.

name: Safdarjung Tomb
description: The last grand enclosed garden-tomb of the Mughal Empire, built in 1754 with ornate domed towers, marble detailing, and water pavilions.
history: Erected in 1754 by Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula for his father, Mirza Muqim Abul Mansur Khan (popularly known as Safdarjung), who was the powerful Subadar of Awadh and Prime Minister to Mughal Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur. Built in the late Charbagh style, the tomb represents the final expression of classic Mughal monumental architecture before imperial power fragmented into regional dynasties.

name: Agrasen ki Baoli
description: A 60-meter long and 15-meter wide 14th-century historical stepwell featuring 108 stone steps arranged across three levels with arched niches.
history: Believed to have been originally commissioned by the legendary King Agrasen of the solar dynasty and reconstructed during the 14th-century Tughlaq or Lodi era. The stepwell functioned as both a water reservoir during seasonal droughts and a cool subterranean sanctuary for travelers and community gatherings. Its striking symmetrical stone arches make it one of Delhi's most celebrated architectural landmarks.

name: Jantar Mantar
description: An open-air astronomical observatory consisting of 13 architectural masonry instruments designed to track celestial movements and calculate solar time.
history: Constructed in 1724 by Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur on the orders of Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah to revise and verify astronomical tables (Zij) and track the orbits of the sun, moon, and planets. Key instruments include the massive Samrat Yantra (giant sundial accurate to two seconds), Jai Prakash Yantra, Ram Yantra, and Misra Yantra. It remains a marvel of 18th-century scientific engineering.

location: Sansad Marg, Connaught Place, New Delhi
best_time: October to March (Midday when sundials cast clear solar shadows)

history: Constructed in 1506 AD by Daulat Khan during the reign of Sultan Sikandar Lodi. The name 'Rajon ki Baoli' derives from the masons (raj-mistris) who used its chambers. The complex includes an adjoining mosque and a canopy tomb with incised plaster decoration, representing refined late-Sultanate water-management architecture.

name: Sanjay Lake
description: A vast 17-hectare artificial freshwater lake surrounded by a 69-hectare green woodland park that serves as a vital ecological and recreational lung for East Delhi.
history: Developed in the 1970s by the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) to capture and manage urban rainwater runoff and create a recreational wetland ecosystem. It regularly attracts over 50 species of resident and migratory waterfowl, including spot-billed ducks, shovellers, common teals, and pintails during winter months. A modern adventure sports park and waterfront promenade were integrated to promote eco-tourism.

description: One of Delhi's largest natural oxbow lakes formed by the meandering Yamuna River, featuring water sports, boating, and wetland ecology.
history: Originally formed hundreds of years ago as an oxbow lake by the changing natural course of the Yamuna River. In the late 20th century, the Delhi Administration developed water sports, kayaking, and a golf course around its banks. The wetland is being revived through extensive ecological restoration to re-establish native aquatic flora, recharge groundwater, and support winter migratory birds.

Named reminiscently after the famous lake in Nainital, it features weeping willows along the banks, aerating fountains that maintain water quality, and an evening-lit paved running track popular with residents.

name: Hauz Khas Lake & Royal Tank (Hauz-i-Alai)
description: A monumental medieval lake and royal reservoir flanked by the two-storey madrasa, pavilions, and the tomb of Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
history: Excavated in 1295 AD by Sultan Alauddin Khilji under the name 'Hauz-i-Alai' (Royal Tank) to supply drinking water to the nearby Siri Fort garrison. Silted up by the mid-14th century, Sultan Firoz Shah Tughlaq desilted the reservoir around 1352 AD, constructing a magnificent L-shaped theological Islamic seminary (Madrasa) and his own sandstone tomb along its eastern and northern shores. In the modern era, the lake was revitalized with aerating bio-remediation systems.

description: A historic natural lake restored into a lush wetland sanctuary using constructed bio-filtering wetland systems and native flora.
history: Historically served as an essential freshwater depression capturing runoff from the South Delhi Aravalli Ridge to supply drinking water to Rajput rulers in Qila Rai Pithora. In 2014–2016, following degradation from road construction, Delhi Development Authority and scientists from the Centre for Environmental Management of Degraded Ecosystems (CEMDE) implemented constructed wetlands that naturally treat millions of liters of water per day, converting it into a thriving wetland habitat for kingfishers and cormorants.

history: Formed naturally in the late 1980s when abandoned silica and red-sand open-pit mining quarries accumulated deep groundwater and monsoon rainwater. Following the closure of mining and the establishment of the Asola Bhatti Wildlife Sanctuary in 1991, the Delhi Forest Department and Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) conserved these water bodies as vital watering grounds for leopards, golden jackals, striped hyenas, and blackbucks.

description: A sprawling trans-boundary seasonal lake and wetland on the Delhi-Haryana border hosting hundreds of thousands of migratory birds.
history: Historically a massive natural lake covering over 220 square kilometers that received overflow from the Sahibi River and drained into the Yamuna. Documented by British surveyor Major Colvin in the 1830s, the wetland once hosted Siberian cranes, flamingos, and pelicans. In recent years, environmental tribunals and wetland conservation authorities have designated it as a protected trans-boundary eco-sensitive wetland.

name: Surajkund Lake (Sun Pool)
description: A 10th-century semi-circular amphitheatre-shaped stepped stone reservoir built in the backdrop of the Aravalli hills, famous for the annual International Crafts Mela.
history: Constructed in the 10th century by Tomar King Suraj Pal, whose family worshipped the Sun God (Surya). Built with stepped stone masonry rising like a Roman amphitheatre, it was engineered to capture rainwater cascading down the Aravalli hills. An ancient Sun Temple stood near its western embankment. It hosts the internationally renowned Surajkund International Crafts Mela every February.

history: Originally developed around the tombs of Mohammed Shah (1444) and Sikandar Lodi (1517), as well as the Sheesh Gumbad and Bara Gumbad. In 1936, the British landscaped the area as 'Lady Willingdon Park'. Following Independence, legendary landscape architect Joseph Allen Stein and Garrett Eckbo remodeled it in 1968 into a botanical public garden featuring the Athpula (eight-piered) bridge built during Akbar's reign.

history: Established during the Mughal era in the 16th century as 'Azim Bagh'. In the early 20th century during the construction of New Delhi, the British converted it into a nursery ('Sunder Nursery') to propagate saplings for Lutyens' Delhi avenues. Between 2007 and 2018, the Aga Khan Trust for Culture (AKTC) transformed the site into Delhi's premier ecological heritage arboretum, conserving monuments like Sunderwala Burj and Lakkarwala Burj.

history: Established in 2004 through a joint ecological restoration initiative by the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and Delhi University CEMDE under Prof. C.R. Babu. Formerly heavily mined and infested with invasive Vilayati Kikar (Prosopis juliflora), it has been transformed into a self-sustaining native forest harboring over 200 species of native trees, shrubs, and rich wildlife including nilgai, porcupines, and 190+ bird species.

history: Developed in 2002 by the DDA in collaboration with the CEMDE to restore degraded floodplains of the Yamuna River. After Independence, colonial statues from across New Delhi, including the 70-foot tall marble statue of King George V, were relocated here.

history: Occupies part of the historical territory of Jahanpanah ('Refuge of the World'), the fourth medieval city of Delhi established in 1326–1327 by Muhammad bin Tughlaq to bridge Siri Fort and Qila Rai Pithora. Protected and maintained by the DDA, this preserved urban forest is densely populated with native Keekar, Neem, and Peepal trees, providing refuge to peacocks, nilgai, and migratory birds.

history: Dates back to the Mughal period when it featured a natural tank (Tal) shaped like a bowl (Katora) and served as an imperial campsite. In 1738, the historic Battle of Delhi between the Maratha Empire led by Peshwa Baji Rao I and the Mughal forces took place here. In modern times, the NDMC developed it into an ornamental garden featuring blooming flowerbeds and the adjacent Talkatora Indoor Stadium.

history: Laid out in 1650 by Princess Roshanara Begum, the brilliant younger daughter of Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal. After supporting Aurangzeb during the war of succession, she retired to this garden palace where her open marble-pillared tomb remains today. In 1928, the historic Roshanara Club within the gardens witnessed the founding of the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI).

Combining classic Islamic four-quadrant canal architecture with tiered circular English herbaceous terraces, it features East and West lawns, the Purdah Garden, Musical Garden, and Circular Sunken Garden. In January 2023, it was officially renamed 'Amrit Udyan' as part of Azadi ka Amrit Mahotsav.

Created as a global pioneering example of waste management under the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, sculptors fabricated life-size models of the Taj Mahal, Eiffel Tower, Statue of Liberty, Leaning Tower of Pisa, Christ the Redeemer, Colosseum, and Great Pyramid using scrap automobile parts, discarded iron sheets, and rusted pipes.

Built under the theme 'Waste to Wealth', artists used discarded vehicle parts, iron grills, and scrap metal to recreate monuments such as the Sun Temple of Konark, Qutub Minar, Hawa Mahal, Khajuraho Temple, Gateway of India, and Meenakshi Temple, powered exclusively through solar energy.

history: Laid out in 1653 by Aizz-un-Nisa Begum, one of Shah Jahan's consorts, following the formal Kashmiri Mughal Charbagh design. It served as a royal country retreat along the Grand Trunk Road. Following his victory in the battle of succession, Emperor Aurangzeb held his grand imperial coronation ceremony here on 31 July 1658. history: Encompasses the oldest continuously inhabited layer of Delhi, spanning the Rajput Tomar dynasty, the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughal Empire, and British colonial outposts. Prominent structures include the 13th-century Tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din Balban (first true arch in India), Jamali Kamali Mosque and Tomb (1528), Metcalfe's Folly, and Rajon ki Baoli. Developed into a contiguous heritage park by DDA and INTACH.

It is a habitat for jackals, nilgai, snakes, and over 150 species of resident and winter migrant birds.

history: Created around the Okhla Barrage constructed across the Yamuna River in 1874. Declared a protected bird sanctuary in 1990 under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972. The expansive shallow wetlands, reed beds, and open water bodies serve as a globally recognized Important Bird and Biodiversity Area (IBA), hosting large flocks of northern pintails, bar-headed geese, grebes, and vulnerable Indian skimmers during winter migration.

history: Hauz-i-Shamsi was excavated in 1229 AD by Sultan Shams-ud-din Iltutmish following a dream where Prophet Muhammad guided him to a freshwater spring marked by a winged horse's hoofprint. In the late 15th century during the Lodi era, the Jahaz Mahal ('Ship Palace') was built alongside its banks as an inn (serai) for pilgrims and royal retreat. It serves as the primary stage for the annual Phool Walon Ki Sair communal harmony festival.

history: Originally constructed by Mughal Emperor Akbar Shah II in 1820 near the revered dargah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki in Mehrauli. In 1842, his son and the last Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar II reconstructed the monumental red sandstone gateway (Hathi Gate) to accommodate royal elephant processions during the annual Phool Walon Ki Sair festival. An empty marble burial plot between the tombs of earlier emperors remains as Zafar died in exile in Rangoon.

history: Constructed in 1303 AD by Sultan Alauddin Khilji as the second city of Delhi to defend against Mongol hordes led by Targhi. Legend holds that the severed heads (sar) of thousands of defeated Mongol soldiers were embedded into the foundation mortar of the fort walls, giving the fort its name. Today, the massive rubble-masonry ramparts stand within open green wooded parklands adjacent to the Siri Fort Sports Complex.

history: Inaugurated on 6 November 2005 by Pramukh Swami Maharaj, President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, and Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. Constructed according to Vastu Shastra and Pancharatra Shastra without using structural steel, the central mandir stands 141 feet high and features 234 ornately carved pillars, 9 domes, and 20,000 murtis of spiritual sages. It houses the Sahaj Anand water show and Hall of Values (Sahajanand Darshan).

In 1664, the Eighth Sikh Guru, Guru Har Krishan Ji, resided here during a smallpox and cholera epidemic, providing clean well-water to heal afflicted citizens before contracting the illness himself. Sardar Baghel Singh built the shrine in 1783 following the capture of Delhi.

name: Jama Masjid (Masjid-i-Jahan-Numa)
description: One of the largest and most magnificent mosques in India, featuring three grand marble domes, two 40-meter minarets, and a courtyard holding 25,000 worshippers.
history: Commissioned in 1650 by Emperor Shah Jahan and inaugurated in 1656 by Syed Abdul Ghafoor Shah Bukhari, whom the Emperor invited from Bukhara to serve as the Shahi Imam. Built by 5,000 workers at a cost of 1 million rupees, it was designed with red sandstone and white marble strips, positioned atop a high natural rocky hill (Bhojla Pahari) overlooking Shahjahanabad.

history: Established in 1783 by Sikh military general Sardar Baghel Singh to commemorate the supreme sacrifice of the Ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, who was publicly martyred on 11 November 1675 under Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb for defending the religious freedom of Kashmiri Pandits. name: India Gate (All India War Memorial)
description: A 42-meter high triumphal archway honoring 84,000 soldiers of the British Indian Army who gave their lives in World War I and the Third Anglo-Afghan War.
history: Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, its foundation stone was laid on 10 February 1921 by Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught, and inaugurated in February 1931 by Viceroy Lord Irwin. Its red Bharatpur stone walls are inscribed with 13,300 fallen soldiers' names. In 1972, following the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971, the Amar Jawan Jyoti eternal flame was installed beneath the arch by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

history: Dedicated to the nation on 25 February 2019 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Designed as four concentric circular chakras representing values of the armed forces: Amar Chakra (Circle of Immortality with eternal flame), Veerta Chakra (Circle of Bravery with bronze battle murals), Tyag Chakra (Circle of Sacrifice inscribed with 26,000+ martyrs' names), and Raksha Chakra (Circle of Protection ringed by 600 trees).

Constructed in 1325 and expanded by Mughal rulers, the courtyard also houses the marble tombs of poet Amir Khusrau (father of Qawwali and Hindavi poetry) and Mughal princess Jahanara Begum. history: Believed to be one of five historic temples founded by the Pandavas following the Mahabharata War. Reconstructed in 1724 by Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur alongside the construction of Jantar Mantar. Since 1 August 1964, the temple has maintained unbroken, continuous 24-hour chanting of the sacred mantra, recognized by the Guinness Book of World Records.

history: Built between 1927 and 1931, designed by British architect Henry Medd who won the Viceroy's design competition. Opened for public worship on 18 January 1931 by Viceroy Lord Irwin. Designed to keep the interior cool during harsh Delhi summers with thick red sandstone arches and recessed windows, it features an oil replica of Caravaggio's 'The Entombment of Christ' presented by Lord Irwin.

The cathedral features an imposing facade with white ionic pillars, a towering curved belfry, and a canopy supported by carved marble columns donated by the Count of Sir Francis. history: Commissioned by Colonel James Skinner of the famed 'Skinner's Horse' cavalry regiment. Skinner made a vow on the battlefield in 1800 while lying wounded that if he survived, he would build a church to God. Designed by Major Robert Smith and consecrated in 1836, the church survived intense bombardments during the 1857 Rebellion and houses historical brass plaques and Skinner's family vault.

history: Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and completed in 1929 as the Viceroy's House following the decision to shift the British Indian capital from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911. Integrating Western classical orders with Indian elements (chattris, jaalis, and elephant motifs), the palace transitioned to become Government House in 1947 and Rashtrapati Bhavan upon the presidency of Dr. Rajendra Prasad in 1950.

It hosted the historic debates of the Constituent Assembly and the birth of India's Constitution on 26 January 1950. In May 2023, the modern triangular New Parliament House was dedicated to the nation by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with the historic building designated as 'Samvidhan Sadan'.

history: Established in 1949 following a landmark exhibition of Indian art at Burlington House in London. The foundation stone of the present Janpath building was laid by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on 12 May 1955. Famous masterworks include the 4,500-year-old bronze 'Dancing Girl' from Mohenjo-daro, Holy Relics of Lord Buddha from Piprahwa, and exquisite Chola bronze sculptures.

It features 35,000 rare artifacts including tribal paintings, woodcarvings, terracottas, bronzes, textiles, and authentic recreated mud-huts representing diverse regional Indian states.

After Independence, it served as the official residence of India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, for 16 years until 1964. history: Originally the palatial residence of industrialist G.D. Birla. Mahatma Gandhi stayed here from 9 September 1947 until his assassination on 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Godse while walking to his evening prayer assembly. Acquired by the Government of India in 1971 and opened as a national memorial in 1973, it preserves Gandhi's bedroom, his personal belongings, the Footsteps of Peace pathway, and the Martyr's Column.

name: Gyarah Murti (11 Statues Dandi March Memorial)
description: A landmark bronze sculpture on Mother Teresa Crescent depicting Mahatma Gandhi leading 10 diverse Indian freedom fighters during the 1930 Salt March.
history: Sculpted by acclaimed Indian master sculptor Debi Prasad Roy Choudhury. The monumental bronze sculpture portrays Mahatma Gandhi striding boldly at the head of the Salt Satyagraha of 1930, followed by ten figures representing diverse facets of Indian society (including a woman, peasant, turbaned Sikh, Muslim, Hindu, and youth), symbolizing collective national resistance against colonial salt laws.
famous_view: Full side profile view of Mahatma Gandhi leading the ten sculpted freedom fighters along the rocky crest against sunset colors.
location: Sardar Patel Marg / Mother Teresa Crescent junction, New Delhi
best_time: October to March (Late afternoon golden hour for bronze sculpture photography)
source: New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) / Ministry of Culture

name: Daryaganj Sunday Book Market (Mahila Haat)
description: Delhi's legendary open-air Sunday book market stretching across the courtyard of Mahila Haat, offering millions of rare, vintage, and discounted books.
history: Started over five decades ago along the pedestrian pavements of Netaji Subhash Marg and Asaf Ali Road in Daryaganj. Reorganized in 2019 by the Municipal Corporation to the modern open-air pedestrian plaza of Mahila Haat opposite Broadway Hotel. It remains an iconic cultural institution where bibliophiles, students, and collectors browse through scholarly texts, vintage classics, and rare collectibles.
famous_view: Vibrant rows of wooden book stalls and reading tables filled with avid book lovers browsing classic volumes on Sunday morning.
location: Mahila Haat, Asaf Ali Road, Daryaganj, Old Delhi
best_time: Sundays only (9:00 AM – 2:00 PM for the best book discoveries)
source: Daryaganj Patri Kitab Kalyan Samiti / MCD

name: Chandni Chowk (Shahjahanabad Heritage Promenade)
description: A historic 17th-century bustling market avenue redesigned with pedestrianized red-granite plazas, street cuisine alleys, and traditional bazaars.
history: Designed in 1650 by Princess Jahanara Begum, the favorite daughter of Emperor Shah Jahan. The original avenue featured a central reflective canal reflecting the silver moonlight ('Chandni'). Connecting the Red Fort Lahori Gate to Fatehpuri Mosque, it evolved into Asia's premier wholesale trade and street food corridor (famous for Paranthe Wali Gali, Dariba Kalan jewelry, and Khari Baoli spice market). In 2021, the 1.3-km stretch was revamped into a pedestrianized heritage zone.
famous_view: Pedestrianized red-granite promenade looking west toward the historic sandstone domes of Fatehpuri Mosque with non-motorized cycle rickshaws.
location: Old Delhi (From Red Fort to Fatehpuri Masjid)
best_time: October to March (Morning 10:00 AM – 1:00 PM or evening culinary food walks)

name: Connaught Place (CP / Rajiv Chowk)
description: Delhi's financial and commercial nerve center, featuring grand Georgian-style circular white colonnades, flagship stores, underground markets, and cafes.
history: Constructed between 1929 and 1933, designed by British architect Robert Tor Russell and named after Prince Arthur, 1st Duke of Connaught. Modeled after the Royal Crescent in Bath, England, it is laid out as two concentric circular rings (Inner and Outer Circles) with radial avenues. It houses India's first underground air-conditioned market, Palika Bazaar (opened in 1978), and remains one of the world's premier heritage business districts.
famous_view: The sweeping white Palladian colonnades of the Inner Circle converging toward Central Park's monumental flag.
location: Connaught Place (Rajiv Chowk), New Delhi
best_time: Year-round (Afternoon shopping 12:00 PM – 4:00 PM or evening cafe dining 6:00 PM – 10:00 PM)

name: Dilli Haat INA
description: An open-air handicraft and food village showcasing regional crafts, handloom weavers, and authentic cuisine from all 28 states of India.
history: Jointly established in March 1994 by Delhi Tourism (DTTDC), Ministry of Textiles, and Ministry of Tourism. Designed by Pradeep Sachdeva with exposed brick and slate roofing to recreate a traditional rural village marketplace (Haat). Craftsmen and artisans are rotated on a bi-weekly basis to ensure diverse regional representation across silk, woodcraft, brassware, and authentic state food stalls.
famous_view: Vibrant brick-paved open central courtyard framed by traditional thatched craft stalls and colorful hanging lamps.
location: Sri Aurobindo Marg, Opposite INA Market, South Delhi
best_time: October to March (11:00 AM – 9:30 PM for shopping and regional dinners)
source: Delhi Tourism and Transportation Development Corporation (DTTDC)

name: Dilli Haat Pitampura
description: A spacious 7.2-acre cultural and craft bazaar in North West Delhi featuring modern amphitheaters, artisan stalls, and dining courts.
history: Inaugurated in April 2008 by DTTDC as the second Dilli Haat in the capital, designed by architect Pradeep Sachdeva. Featuring contemporary architectural canopies, an open-air amphitheatre holding 450 people, craft shops, and food courts, it hosts national handloom expos, mango festivals, and cultural performances.
famous_view: Curved brick plaza under decorative fabric canopies with the illuminated Pitampura TV Tower in the background.
location: Netaji Subhash Place, Pitampura, North West Delhi
best_time: October to March (Evenings 4:00 PM – 9:00 PM)

name: Dilli Haat Janakpuri
description: The largest and most modern Dilli Haat, spanning 9.6 acres in West Delhi with striking music pavilions, bamboo courtyards, and craft stalls.
history: Inaugurated in June 2014 by DTTDC. Designed with an emphasis on sustainable music-and-craft tourism, it features an 800-seat outdoor amphitheatre, an indoor air-conditioned auditorium, 100 craft shops, themed food courts, and large open lawns hosting musical festivals and culinary melas.
famous_view: The grand musical open-air amphitheatre and geometric bamboo canopy towers illuminated at dusk.
location: Lal Sai Mandir Marg, Janakpuri, West Delhi
best_time: October to March (Evenings 4:30 PM – 9:30 PM)

name: India Habitat Centre (IHC)
description: A premier multidisciplinary cultural and arts complex featuring open atrium courtyards, art galleries, amphitheaters, and visual arts exhibitions.
history: Designed by celebrated architect Joseph Allen Stein and completed in 1993. Spanning 9 acres, the complex is internationally acclaimed for its bioclimatic design, utilizing vertical brick louvers, open green atriums, and shading overhangs to temper Delhi's climate naturally. It is a vibrant hub for film festivals, art exhibitions, literary debates, and theatrical performances.
famous_view: The sun-shaded open brick atrium courtyard with Stein's signature overhead blue louvers and sculptural water features.
location: Lodhi Road, New Delhi
best_time: Year-round (10:00 AM – 8:00 PM for art exhibitions and live events)
